docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM S Pole, 45 deg, Count
docs.description: This shot count data file is applicable to the LRO LOLA DEM S Pole, 45 deg, version 4. This raster dataset represents a LOLA shot count for each pixel in the original polar LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Along with each gridded DEM, a "count" image is created which reports, at the chosen resolution, how many LOLA shots intersected that pixel. If there are more than one shot per pixel, the mean of the shots is used per pixel. Where no LOLA shots are available, the pixel is approximated using a spline interpolation from the surrounding neighbors.

docs.title: LRO LROC Image Mosaic, Malapert Massif
LRO Narrow Angle Camera, Mosaic Hermite A
docs.description:
Hermite-A is one of the potential NASA Resource Prospector landing sites used to study mission design and feasibility. RP will be the first lunar surface robotic expedition to explore the character and feasibility of in situ resource utilization at the lunar poles. It is aimed at determining where, and how much, hydrogen-bearing and other volatiles are sequestered in polar cold traps. To meet its goals, the mission should land where the likelihood of finding polar volatiles is high. In addition to a high potential of volatile sequestration, a landing site candidate must meet engineering and mission operations requirements: sufficient solar access to power the rover over mission lifetime, sufficient visibility to ground stations for real time communications, manageable hazards such as slopes and block abundance, etc. A landing site must have acceptable slopes within the 3- sigma landing ellipse (200-m diameter); it should also have at least 48 hours of sun and DTE communications access to accommodate checkout, rover egress, and initial operations, with margin. RP’s Automated Traverse Search Tool has been applied to Hermite-A region, finding numerous potential traverses.

This layer is a merge and crop from the North Pole NAC mosaic. It is at 1 m/pixel with Oblique Stereographic projection.

docs.title: Unified Global Geologic Map of the Moon, Geologic Contacts
docs.description: Map description: This new work represents a seamless, globally consistent, 1:5,000,000-scale geologic map derived from the six digitally renovated geologic maps (see Source Online Linkage below). The goal of this project was to create a digital resource for science research and analysis, future geologic mapping efforts, be it local-, regional-, or global-scale products, and as a resource for the educators and the public interested in lunar geology. Here we present the completed mapping project as unit contacts, geologic unit polygons, linear features, and unit and feature nomenclature annotation. The product overlies shaded-relief products derived from SELENE Kaguya terrain camera stereo (equatorial, ˜60 m/pix) and LOLA altimetry (north and south polar, 100 m/pix). These data are not included with this download due to size considerations, but a readme in the Lunar_Raster folder provides the download links. This download page includes a PDF of the geologic map (right-side) with a brief Description of Map Units and Explanation of Map Symbols, as well as a JPG of the map for quick access viewing. This release is subject to update based on community feedback and peer-review. Version 2 updates: Two errors were addressed in this update: (1) Large area polygons were offset from their contacts, likely due to user error. Polygons were rebuilt to fix the issue and post processing (dissolving, reattributing, etc.) to rectify the aesthetic of the map. (2) Contacts were not visible but should have been due to incorrect labeling as DND (do not draw). Those that needed to be drawn have been reattributed as “certain” those that are not drawn are labeled as “internal”. Additionally, in version 1 of this data, crater polygons with similar attributes had been dissolved and lumped into contiguous units. This has been changed so that all craters are now discrete units. This adds ˜1000 units to the GeoUnits feature class and the related contacts are now visible and labeled as “certain”. Suggested citation: Fortezzo, C.M., Spudis, P. D. and Harrel, S. L. (2020). Release of the Digital Unified Global Geologic Map of the Moon At 1:5,000,000- Scale. Paper presented at the 51st Lunar and Planetary Science Conference, Lunar and Planetary Institute, Houston, TX. https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2020/pdf/2760.pdf This map is for viewing purposes only. GIS files for this composite map can be found on the USGS Astropedia Lunar and Planetary Cartographic Catalog. Please note, this is not a USGS SIM. Map title: Unified Global Geologic Map of the Moon USGS Map Number: N/A Scale: 1:5M Authors: Fortezzo, C.M., Spudis, P. D. and Harrel, S. L. Publication date: 2020 Link to original map source: https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/Moon/Geology/Unified_Geologic_Map_of_the_Moon_GIS_v2

docs.title: LRO NAC Mosaic 0.5mpp, Philolaus, N Pole
docs.description: This is a visible image mosaic generated using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) images from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission. The images were orthorectified using a digital elevation model (DEM) created from LROC NAC stereo images, when available, or LRO's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) global DEM. The mosaic is generated at the same resolution at which the individual LROC NAC images were gathered, which is approximately 0.5 meters/pixel. The mosaic was registered horizontally to the LOLA global DEM and projected to a north polar stereographic projection.

docs.title: LRO NAC Orthoimage 0.66mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site Q
docs.description: This is an orthorectified LRO NAC image generated using AMES Stereo Pipeline and ISIS4. This data uses the NACs M110670656 and M110691019 as stereo image input. Output ortho image is sampled at 0.66mpp. Downloaded data is in a site centered orthographic projection. Data was created by: Heather Lethcoe at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

docs.title: LRO NAC Mosaic 0.67mpp, Malapert Massif
docs.description: This mage mosaic of the Malapert Massif region on the Moon's south pole was produced with USGS ISIS software from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) imagery. Each NAC image was horizontally coregistered to the Wide Angle Camera (WAC) basemap and, where available, to neighboring NAC images of similar resolution. The final mosaic was exported from ArcGIS Pro at 67 cm/px in a south polar stereographic projection. Created by Tobey Miner during his 2026 summer internship at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

docs.title: LRO NAC Color Hillshade 2.4mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site C
docs.description: This is an LRO (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter) NAC (Narrow Angle Camera) Color Hillshade generated from the corresponding DEM produced using AMES Stereo Pipeline and ISIS4. Hillshade was generated and color scheme has been applied using ArcGIS Pro. Downloaded data is in a site centered orthographic projection. Data was created by: Heather Lethcoe at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

docs.title: LRO NAC Hillshade 2.4mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site C

docs.title: LRO NAC Orthoimage 0.79mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site C
docs.description: This is an orthorectified LRO (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter) NAC (Narrow Angle Camera) image generated using AMES Stereo Pipeline and ISIS4. This data has been generated to resolve the Endurance-A Site <> at a higher resolution. Downloaded data is in a site centered orthographic projection. Data was created by: Heather Lethcoe at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

docs.title: LRO NAC Crater Detections 0.83mpp, Endurance-A Concept Site Q
docs.description: This is an imagery mosaic of LRO NAC images that were used to generate crater detections for the Endurance-A Site Q region on the south pole of the moon. The crater detection tool takes a hybrid approach, which blends traditional computer vision techniques with deep learning. The input image is subsampled to various resolutions such that the base of the pyramid is the image at its highest resolution, and the apex of the pyramid is the image at its lowest resolution. The purpose for this structure is twofold; It allows for detection of craters at various sizes and it substantially decreases the processing time when searching for large craters. The output of tool includes a georeferenced image with craters labeled by bounding boxes.

docs.title: LRO , DEM Error Hermite-A
docs.description: This layer depicts terrain error associated with the Hermite-A Photoclinometrically-enhanced Stereo Terrain File. The only way to 'measure' the error of this terrain is relative to the much sparser LOLA terrain. In doing so, the Resource Prospector team found the mean absolute error from the LOLA DEM is 0.54 meters, while the standard deviation is 0.66 meters. The individual pixel errors are plotted in this 'error file'. It is evident that the major deviations are where there are LOLA artifacts from erroneous tracks. This means that the major source of 'error' is actually the photoclinometry algorithm 'correcting' LOLA in these locations.

docs.title: LRO NAC Mosaic 1mpp, N Pole
docs.description:
This product is an uncontrolled mosaic of LROC NAC images of the North pole of the Moon, projected in Polar Stereographic with a scale of 1 m/px at the pole. The mosaic has a latitude range of 85.5 degrees to 90 degrees and is stored as 40 map tiles. The tiles are in latitudinal bands of 1 degrees, except for the polar tiles, which cover 1.5 degrees of latitude. There are four tiles in the first band (88.5 degrees to 90 degrees latitude), eight in the second (87.5 degrees to 88.5 degrees latitude), twelve in the third (86.5 degrees to 87.5 degrees latitude), and sixteen in the fourth (85.5 degrees to 86.5 degrees latitude). Due to the tilt of the Moon's spin axis (1.54 degrees), some regions near the poles are in permanent shadow while other nearby regions remain illuminated for the majority of the year. This subtle tilt causes lighting changes from lunation to lunation. The poles are most illuminated at their respective summer solstice. Thus images for this NAC north pole mosaic were acquired during the northern solstice (2010-07-23 through 2010-12-11), and layered in order of the greatest incidence angle and sub-solar latitude closest to the pole. All NAC images were map projected onto the LOLA polar DEM, sampled at 100 m/px, using the LOLA crossover-corrected ephemeris. All tiles use the same polar stereographic projection so they can be combined into a seamless mosaic without reprojection. The images were not registered to one another. The combined mosaic of these tiles has been manually tiepointed to the current basemap layer LRO LROC WAC Image Mosaic, N Pole.
When citing this product, use the following reference: Wagner, R. V., Speyerer, E. J., Robinson, M. S., & LROC Team. (2015). New Mosaicked Data Products from the LROC Team. In Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (Vol. 46, abstract #1473). https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2015/pdf/1473.pdf

docs.title: LRO NAC Mosaic 1mpp, S Pole
docs.description:
This product is an uncontrolled mosaic of LROC NAC images of the South pole of the Moon, projected in Polar Stereographic with a scale of 1 m/px at the pole. The mosaic has a latitude range of 85.5 degrees to 90 degrees and is stored as 40 map tiles. The tiles are in latitudinal bands of 1 degrees, except for the polar tiles, which cover 1.5 degrees of latitude. There are four tiles in the first band (88.5 degrees to 90 degrees latitude), eight in the second (87.5 degrees to 88.5 degrees latitude), twelve in the third (86.5 degrees to 87.5 degrees latitude), and sixteen in the fourth (85.5 degrees to 86.5 degrees latitude). Due to the tilt of the Moon's spin axis (1.54 degrees), some regions near the poles are in permanent shadow while other nearby regions remain illuminated for the majority of the year. This subtle tilt causes lighting changes from lunation to lunation. The poles are most illuminated at their respective summer solstice. Thus images for this NAC south pole mosaic were acquired during the southern solstice (2010-07-23 through 2010-12-11), and layered in order of the greatest incidence angle and sub-solar latitude closest to the pole. All NAC images were map projected onto the LOLA polar DEM, sampled at 100 m/px, using the LOLA crossover-corrected ephemeris. All tiles use the same polar stereographic projection so they can be combined into a seamless mosaic without reprojection. The images were not registered to one another. The combined mosaic of these tiles has been manually tiepointed to the current basemap layer LRO LROC WAC Image Mosaic, S Pole.
When citing this product, use the following reference: Wagner, R. V., Speyerer, E. J., Robinson, M. S., & LROC Team. (2015). New Mosaicked Data Products from the LROC Team. In Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (Vol. 46, abstract #1473). https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2015/pdf/1473.pdf

docs.title: LRO NAC Post-Landing Ortho Mosaic 1mpp, IM-1 Landing Site
docs.description: This is a visible image mosaic for the Intuitive Machines IM-1 Nova-C, known as Odysseus, lander and includes the NAC image (M1463440322L) acquired after landing. This product has been generated using USGS ISIS software from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) imagery. Images in this mosaic have been orthorectified and mosaicked together using ArcGIS Pro. The additional NAC image (M1463440322L), depicting the lander on the surface, is not orthorectified and it has only  been tiepointed to the ortho-mosaic. Data is in an orthographic projection and the mosaic is centered at 80.13S 1.44E. NAC with lander data source: https://www.lroc.asu.edu/posts/1360. Trek mosaic dataset creator: Heather Lethcoe at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (hlethcoe@jpl.nasa.gov).

docs.title: LRO Narrow Angle Camera, Optimally-lit Mosaic Hermite A
docs.description:
Hermite-A is one of the potential NASA Resource Prospector landing sites used to study mission design and feasibility. RP will be the first lunar surface robotic expedition to explore the character and feasibility of in situ resource utilization at the lunar poles. It is aimed at determining where, and how much, hydrogen-bearing and other volatiles are sequestered in polar cold traps. To meet its goals, the mission should land where the likelihood of finding polar volatiles is high. In addition to a high potential of volatile sequestration, a landing site candidate must meet engineering and mission operations requirements: sufficient solar access to power the rover over mission lifetime, sufficient visibility to ground stations for real time communications, manageable hazards such as slopes and block abundance, etc. A landing site must have acceptable slopes within the 3- sigma landing ellipse (200-m diameter); it should also have at least 48 hours of sun and DTE communications access to accommodate checkout, rover egress, and initial operations, with margin. RP’s Automated Traverse Search Tool has been applied to Hermite-A region, finding numerous potential traverses.
 
The optimally-lit mosaic was assembled from inspecting 800 NAC images and selecting 22 that provided the best lighting conditions for this scene. In turn, the best pixels from those images were mosaicked together to create the resulting mosaic. The mosaic had to be split it into four regions to keep the image-to-image control coherent, resulting in some potential discontinuities.

LRO LOLA Color Hillshade 5 mpp, Site20: Leibnitz Beta Plateau, S Pole
docs.description: This colorized shaded-relief map has been generated from the high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) of the high-priority lunar south pole landing site Leibnitz beta plateau (Site 20). This DEM was generated using exclusively laser altimetry data acquired by LRO-LOLA and through an iterative co-adjustment of the LOLA tracks in a self-consistent fashion. This reduced the orbital errors by over a factor of 10 such that the new track geolocation uncertainty is ˜10 - 20 cm horizontally and ˜2 - 4 cm vertically. This new 5m/px DEM is substantially more realistic than previous ones with fewer artifacts due to orbital errors and fewer spurious noise points. While the fraction of interpolated 5m pixels in these polar LDEMs is necessarily large (˜90%) due to LOLA's cross-track and inter-spot spacing, these LDEMs have the advantage of having accurate geodetic control and of being unaffected by shadows, and, thus, will be useful constraints on higher-resolution topographic models derived from imagery. The elevation values are in meters and are relative to a radius of 1737400m. Please site the following when using this data: Barker, M.K., et al. (2020), Improved LOLA Elevation Maps for South Pole Landing Sites: Error Estimates and Their Impact on Illumination Conditions, Planetary & Space Science, in press, doi:10.1016/j.pss.2020.105119.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color Slope < 10 deg, S Pole, 87.5 deg
docs.description: This is a colorized slope map that was generated from the version 4 of the LRO LOLA DEM, S Pole, 87.5 deg. The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 5 m/px, based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs “surface” and “grdblend”. The DEM was scaled from a 16-bit signed integer to a 32-bit floating point. Slope was generated from this DEM to create this slope product sampled at 5 m/px. Slope values greater than 10 deg were excluded from this data for visualization and analysis purposes. Slope values are in degrees and referred to a radius of 1737400m. The legend conveys the mapping colors to slope values (degrees).

The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 100 meters per pixel, based on altimetry data acquired through Spetember 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs "surface" and "grdblend". Map values are referred to a radius of 1737400 m.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 87.5 deg, Count
docs.description: This shot count data file is applicable to the LRO LOLA DEM N Pole, 87.5 deg, version 4. This raster dataset represents a LOLA shot count for each pixel in the original 128ppd LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Along with each gridded DEM, a “count” image is created which reports, at the chosen resolution, how many LOLA shots intersected that pixel. If there are more than one shot per pixel, the mean of the shots is used per pixel. Where no LOLA shots are available, the pixel is approximated using a spline interpolation from the surrounding neighbors.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 87.5 deg, Coverage
docs.description: This raster data set is a binary (True or False) representation of the original LOLA shot count for each pixel in the LOLA North Pole 87.5 degree, Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Pixels which contain the value zero (False) have no coverage from the LOLA instrument. Pixels which contain the value 1 have coverage for at least one or more LOLA shots. For the LOLA DEM this means where no LOLA shots are available, the pixel is approximated using a spline interpolation from the surrounding neighbors (and thus not as accurate).

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 87.5 deg, Grayscale

This image was generated from the DEM by scaling the elevation values from the range of -5300 to 1925 integer values between 0 and 255. Elevation below and above the -5300 and 1925 are mapped to 0 and 255, respectively.

docs.title: CE-2 CCD Ortho Mosaic, N Pole
docs.description:
China's Chang'e 2 robotic probe was launched from Xichang Satellite Launch Center on 1 October 2010 aboard a Long March 3C rocket. It conducted studies of the Moon’s surface from lunar orbit between October 6 2010 and June 8 2011, prior to continuing its mission at the Earth-Sun L2 Lagrangian point and the asteroid Toutatis. From its working orbit with an altitude of 100 km above the lunar surface, Chang'e 2 was able to produce a global map of the Moon with 7-meter resolution, the highest-resolution map of the entire Moon to have been yet produced. It is this 7-meter data that was used to produce this layer in Moon Trek. Chang'e 2 also worked from an elliptical orbit with a perilune of 15 km and an apolune of apolune, allowing selected areas to be imaged at resolutions as high as 1.3 meters, enabling higher-resolution mapping of areas targeted for future landings.

Chang'e 2’s CCD camera employs a two-line push-broom sensor. The two CCD lines are positioned on separate focal planes, enabling the gathering of forward- and backward-looking imagery along the line of flight. This allows for the simultaneous production of stereo pairs. Both lines consist of 6144 10.1 µm pixels. Because the forward-looking line is closer to the center of the focal plane, it offers better resolution with a viewing angle of 8°, while the rear-looking line has a viewing angle of 17.2°.

On April 4, 2018, the CE-2 Global Digital Orthophoto Model (DOM) dataset with 7m resolution was released by Ground Research and Application System of China Lunar Exploration Program. The dataset is produced using images acquired by CCD stereo cameras onboard CE-2 spacecraft at 100 km orbit, which is divided into 844 map subdivisions. 

Individual map subdivision tiles were mosaicked together and clipped at the north polar region from 90N to 60N. This data has been projected to a stereographic polar projection. This data is an 8-bit unsigned integer with values ranging from 1 to 255 and a no data value of 0.

docs.title: LRO Mini-RF First Stokes Parameter
LRO North Polar Mini-RF Circular Polarization Ratio
LRO North Polar Mini-RF Circular Polarization Ratio, Colorized
LRO Mini-RF CPR 15mpp, Malapert
docs.description:
This is a Mini-RF Circularly Polarized Ratio (CPR) dataset with the 49 degrees equivalent incidence angle trend removed. Data units are in Decibels (db) where bright pixels (greater than 0 db) represent relatively high backscatter and dark pixels (less than 0 db) represent low backscatter.

Mini-RF is a Synthetic Aperture Radar designed in a hybrid dual-polarimetric architecture, transmitting a circularly polarized signal to the lunar surface and receives the horizontal and vertical linear polarizations. The received radar signal from Mini-RF is represented using the four Stokes parameters, which can be combined to derive metrics for lunar surface properties. The monostatic Mini-RF data in the PDS was processed onto a spherical Moon, and the applied Vexcel SAR processor resulted in offsets to the correct selenolocation (see Harris et al., this meeting). As a result, until now, local incidence angles were not known for the monostatic data. We have corrected the position of level-1 monostatic S-band data & re-orthorectified it on to a SLDEM/LOLA shape model. The local incidence angle of each pixel can then be determined. The observed trend in CPR for the monostatic data agrees reasonably well with expectations from Hagfors modeling, at least for i˜35° and ˜70°, with a dielectric permittivity of ˜4.3. Removal of this CPR trend emphasizes deviations from typical scattering properties. Data Credit: https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2023/pdf/1564.pdf

From its working orbit with an altitude of 100 km above the lunar surface, Chang'e 2 was able to produce a global map of the Moon with 7-meter resolution, the highest-resolution map of the entire Moon to have been yet produced. It is this 7-meter data that was used to produce this layer in Moon Trek. Chang'e 2 also worked from an elliptical orbit with a perilune of 15 km and an apolune of apolune, allowing selected areas to be imaged at resolutions as high as 1.3 meters, enabling higher-resolution mapping of areas targeted for future landings.

Chang'e 2’s CCD camera employs a two-line push-broom sensor. The two CCD lines are positioned on separate focal planes, enabling the gathering of forward- and backward-looking imagery along the line of flight. This allows for the simultaneous production of stereo pairs. Both lines consist of 6144 10.1 µm pixels. Because the forward-looking line is closer to the center of the focal plane, it offers better resolution with a viewing angle of 8°, while the rear-looking line has a viewing angle of 17.2°.

On April 4, 2018, the CE-2 Global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) dataset with 20m resolution was released by Ground Research and Application System of China Lunar Exploration Program. The dataset is produced using stereopairs acquired by CCD stereo cameras onboard CE-2 spacecraft at 100km orbit, which is divided into 188 map subdivisions. 

Individual map subdivision tiles were mosaicked together, clipped at the south polar region from 90S to 60S, and projected to a stereographic south polar projection. The DEM was registered horizontally and vertically to LRO's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data. The values for the DEM used to generate this colorized slope product are in meters and referred to a radius of 1737400m. A slope function was applied to the DEM to create this colorized slope product. This data has been processed to exclude slope values > 15 degrees for analysis and visualization purposes. Slope values are in degrees and the legend coveys the mapping colors to slope values.

docs.title: LRO NAC PSR Mosaic 20mpp, N Pole
docs.description: This is an uncontrolled mosaic generated from images taken by the Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) for the North Pole region of the Moon. The NAC mosaics have been trimmed to the Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) shapefile, providing visible NAC image coverage of the PSRs only. Acquisition of NAC PSR observations were optimized over several campaigns to maximize signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), resulting in a comprehensive dataset that is systematically reviewed and analyzed. Observations are acquired at a variety of pixel scales (2 to 20 m/px). The final PSR mosaics are assembled from re-sampled images to 20 m/px, and ordering of images is based on image quality and areal coverage of individual PSRs. A total of 550 NAC images were used to create a North Pole PSR mosaic at 20 m/px, 90° to 80° latitude, and -180° to 180° longitude. This mosaic has been merged with the existing LROC NAC North Pole RDR product to replace over-saturated illuminated polar areas.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 75 deg, ColorHillshade
docs.description: This is version 4 of the LRO LOLA North Pole 75 deg DEM, ColorHillshade. This is a colorized shaded-relief of a original polar LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM). The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 100 meters per pixel, based on altimetry data acquired through Spetember 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs "surface" and "grdblend". Map values are referred to a radius of 1737400 m.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 75 deg, Coverage
docs.description: This raster data set is a binary (True or False) representation of the original LOLA shot count for each pixel in the LOLA North Pole 75 degree, Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Pixels which contain the value zero (False) have no coverage from the LOLA instrument. Pixels which contain the value 1 have coverage for at least one or more LOLA shots. For the LOLA DEM this means where no LOLA shots are available, the pixel is approximated using a spline interpolation from the surrounding neighbors (and thus not as accurate).

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 75 deg, Grayscale
docs.description: This is version 4 of the LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 75 deg, Grayscale. This data product is a grayscale version of the LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 75 deg that is based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. This image was generated from the DEM by scaling the elevation values from the range of -7250 to 3950 integer values between 0 and 255. Elevation below and above the -7250 and 3950 are mapped to 0 and 255, respectively.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Average Earth Visibility, 60 mpp, N Pole
docs.description: This data represents the Earth visibility, averaged over hourly timesteps spanning 18.6 years, for the North Polar region of the Moon. Since our light source is not a point but rather a finite disc, its position and size can be changed to study the visibility of the Earth from the lunar poles rather than the solar input. The extent of this data is 75N-90N and has a resolution of 60 m/px. Pixel values represent the percentage of Earth visibility and the legend coveys the mapping colors to values. When using this data please cite: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography, Icarus, Vol. 211, pp. 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030.

docs.title: Chandrayaan-1 Mini-SAR CPR N Pole
docs.description: This is the Mini-SAR CPR dataset. Mini-SAR combines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) at two wavelengths (S and X band) and two resolutions (150 m and 30 m) with interferometric and communications. Previous radar observations (Earth-based, and one bistatic data set from Clementine) of the permanently shadowed regions of the lunar poles seem to indicate areas of high circular polarization ratio (CPR) consistent with volume scattering from volatile deposits (e.g. water ice) buried at shallow (0.1-1 m) depth. Between mid-February and mid-April, 2009, Mini-SAR mapped more than 95% of the areas polewards of 80° latitude at a resolution of 150 meters. The north polar region displays backscatter properties typical for the Moon, with circular polarization ratio (CPR) values in the range of 0.1-0.3, increasing to over 1.0 for young primary impact craters. These higher CPR values likely reflect surface roughness associated with these fresh features. In contrast, some craters in this region show elevated CPR in their interiors, but not exterior to their rims. Almost all of these features are in permanent sun shadow and correlate with proposed locations of polar ice modeled on the basis of Lunar Prospector neutron data. These relations are consistent with deposits of water ice in these craters. The CPR is derived from the Stokes parameters. This map is not ortho-rectified.

docs.title: Geologic Map of South Pole-Aitken (SPA) Basin and South Pole Region of the Moon
docs.description:
Thorough analysis and synthesis of available image, topographic, and spectral data, have enabled us to derive a comprehensive geological map (mapping scale: 1:500,000) of the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin region. Our map encompasses additional major basins, such as Ingenii, Apollo, Schrodinger, and Orientale basins, that we employed as stratigraphic markers. A variety of plains-forming units were identified from multiple time periods, including light and dark plains from the Nectarian to the Eratosthenian period. Additionally, craters from diverse geological time periods were identified and catalogued. Published absolute model ages were documented and compared to provide a chronology for the stratigraphic units. In the present study, the majority of interpreted stratigraphic geological units are consistent with published absolute model ages. However, inconsistencies between various published studies are also addressed, resulting primarily due to discrepancies in the use of different stratigraphic systems and the derivation of absolute model ages. A variety of scientific questions and issues pertinent to the SPA basin are addressed with our geological map, such as stratigraphic age, morphological and spectral characteristics of the basin, and formation history of the basin. Finally, we establish the context for key targets for sample return and in situ investigation, in light of supporting scientific objectives related to understanding the Moon's early impact history, determining the age of the SPA basin, and volcanism, as well as providing an evaluation of the materials relevant to scientific discovery and resource utilization.

Publication: "Geological Mapping of the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) Basin Region of the Moon." (W. Iqbal, L. Wueller, C.M. Poehler, C.H. van der Bogert, H. Hiesinger, M.A. Ivanov, J. Wright, J.W. Head, A. Oetting and B.L. Jolliff) Icarus, 459, 117234,  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2026.117234

The map plate and geotiff are also publicly available in the IfP Zenodo repository: https://zenodo.org/record/19728952

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color Slope < 10 deg, N Pole
docs.description:
This is a colorized slope map of the version 4 of the LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 45 deg, clipped to approximately 60 degrees so that the data is fully contained within the Trek polar basemap.
This data has been processed to exclude slope values > 10 degrees for analysis and visualization purposes. The DEM used to generate this product is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 100 m/px, based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs "surface" and "grdblend". DEM elevation values are referred to a radius of 1737400 m. Slope values are in degrees and the legend conveys the mapping color to slope values.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM S Pole, 45 deg, No Data Mask
docs.description: This raster data set is a binary (True or False) representation of the original LOLA shot count for each pixel in the LOLA South Pole, 45 degree Digital Elevation Model. Pixels which contain the value zero (False) have no coverage from the LOLA instrument. Pixels which contain the value 1 have coverage for at least one or more LOLA shots. Pixels with the value of zero are set to black. Pixels with the value of 1 are set to transparent. For the LOLA DEM this means where no LOLA shots are available, the pixel is approximated using a spline interpolation from the surrounding neighbors (and thus not as accurate).

The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution 100 meters per pixel, based on altimetry data acquired through Spetember 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs "surface" and "grdblend". Map values are referred to a radius of 1737400 m.

docs.title: LRO LOLA DEM, N Pole, 45 deg, Count
docs.description: This shot count data file is applicable to the LRO LOLA DEM N Pole, 45 deg, version 4. This raster dataset represents a LOLA shot count for each pixel in the original polar LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Along with each gridded DEM, a “count” image is created which reports, at the chosen resolution, how many LOLA shots intersected that pixel. If there are more than one shot per pixel, the mean of the shots is used per pixel. Where no LOLA shots are available, the pixel is approximated using a spline interpolation from the surrounding neighbors.

docs.title: LRO WAC Percentage-Based Illumination 100mpp, N Pole
docs.description: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) provides multi-temporal images of the polar regions, with repeat imaging with the Wide-Angle Camera approximately every 2 hours with a ground sampling distance of 100 meters enabling production of an illumination map from 88 to 90 degrees north. WAC images (n=3548) acquired over one lunar year from 15 February 2010 to 5 February 2011 form the basis of the map. Temporal gaps were filled with 234 observations acquired with virtually identical lighting at other times during the mission. Each image was first map-projected at 100 meters/pixel in polar stereographic projection onto a 30 m LOLA DEM (Smith et al., 2010) using an improved WAC distortion model (Speyerer et al., 2016) and improved spacecraft ephemeris (Mazarico et al., 2011). Binary images indicating the illumination state of each image were created by applying a series of spatial filters and a conservative global threshold. Then the illumination map was derived by taking the number of times a mapped pixel was illuminated over the number of instances the mapped pixel was imaged. This map may contain some biases due to non-uniform timing between observations (Example- WAC images were not acquired on orbits when Mini-RF acquired polar observations). To limit this non-linear effect, an additional time-weighted illumination map is provided that linearly interpolated missed observations (see WAC_POLE_ILL_TWI_NORTH and WAC_POLE_ILL_TWI_SOUTH). For more information on the derivation of these products and for a map of image counts per pixel, see Speyerer and Robinson (2013). Due to a small amount of image noise and scattered light, some regions that are permanently shadowed from direct solar illumination have percentage values that are close to, but not equal to zero. These artifacts in the middle of permanently shadowed regions should be ignored when analyzing the extent. When citing this product, use the following reference: Speyerer, E. J., & Robinson, M. S. (2013). Persistently illuminated regions at the lunar poles: Ideal sites for future exploration. Icarus, 222(1), 122-136. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2012.10.010

docs.title: LRO WAC Time-Weighted Illumination 100mpp, N Pole
docs.description: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) provides multi-temporal images of the polar regions, with repeat imaging with the Wide-Angle Camera approximately every 2 hours with a ground sampling distance of 100 meters enabling production of an illumination map from 88 to 90 degrees north. For more information on the derivation of these products and for a map of image counts per pixel, see Speyerer and Robinson (2013). Each image was first map-projected at 100 meters/pixel in polar stereographic projection onto a 30 m DEM provided by the LOLA team (Smith et al., 2010) using an improved WAC distortion model (Speyerer et al., 2016) and improved spacecraft ephemeris (Mazarico et al., 2011). Binary images indicating the illumination state of each image were created by applying a series of spatial filters and a conservative global threshold. Like the percentage-based illumination maps, this illumination map was derived by taking the number of times a mapped pixel was illuminated over the number of instances the mapped pixel was imaged. However, in order to minimize biases introduced by non-equally spaced observations, images taken during periods of infrequent WAC observations are weighted twice as much as those taken during nominal operations and areas not within the field of view were linearly interpolated based on preceding and subsequent observations where image data was available for a specific mapped pixel. A version of the illumination map without interpolation is archived under WAC_POLE_ILL_PCT_NORTH and WAC_POLE_ILL_PCT_SOUTH. For more information on the derivation of these products and for a map of image counts per pixel, see Speyerer and Robinson (2013). Due to a small amount of image noise and scattered light, some regions that are permanently shadowed from direct solar illumination have percentage values that are close to, but not equal to zero. These artifacts in the middle of permanently shadowed regions should be ignored when analyzing the extent. When citing this product, use the following reference: Speyerer, E. J., & Robinson, M. S. (2013). Persistently illuminated regions at the lunar poles: Ideal sites for future exploration. Icarus, 222(1), 122-136. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2012.10.010

docs.title: Clementine UVVIS Image Mosaic, N Pole
docs.description: The Clementine 750 nm Version 2 mosaic is a grayscale data set representing the albedo (brightness of the lunar surface) as measured at the 750 nm wavelength by the UVVIS camera. This lunar base map is a radiometrically and geometrically controlled, photometrically modeled global image mosaic compiled using more than 43,000 images from the 750 nanometer filter observations of the UVVIS. The Clementine experiment carried four scientific imaging cameras: the Ultraviolet/Visible (UVVIS), Near-Infrared (NIR), High-Resolution (HiRES), and Long-wave Infrared (LWIR) cameras. The Ultraviolet/Visible (UVVIS) camera imaged the surface of the Moon at five wavelengths spanning the ultraviolet to near-infrared spectrum and the Near-Infrared (NIR) camera collected data at six wavelengths extending into the short-wave infrared. This experiment yielded information on the color and inferred compositional properties of lunar soils and surface units, and also provided images useful for morphologic studies and cratering statistics. Most images were taken at low Sun angles, which is useful for compositional studies but not for observing morphology. Global mosaics at the five UVVIS and six NIR coregistered wavelengths were created using nearly 1 million images and are displayed here at a resolution of ~100 m/pixel.

docs.title: LRO Mini-RF CPR N Pole, Color
docs.description: This image is a colorized version of the Mini-RF CPR dataset. Mini-RF combines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) at two wavelengths (S and X band)and two resolutions (150 m and 30 m) with interferometric and communications. Previous radar observations (Earth-based, and one bistatic data set from Clementine) of the permanently shadowed regions of the lunar poles seem to indicate areas of high circular polarization ratio (CPR) consistent with volume scattering from volatile deposits (e.g. water ice) buried at shallow (0.1-1 m) depth. The LRO Mini-RF utilizes new wide band hybrid polarization architecture to measure the Stokes parameters of the reflected signal. These data will help to differentiate 'true' volumetric ice reflections from 'false' returns due to angular surface regolith. Additional lunar science investigations (e.g. pyroclastic deposit characterization) will also be attempted during the LRO extended mission. On orbit calibration procedures for LRO Mini RF have been validated using Chandrayaan 1 and ground based facilities (Arecibo and Greenbank Radio Observatories). The CPR is derived from the Stokes parameters.  This map is not ortho-rectified.

docs.title: LOLA Slope Northpole 120m, Colorized
docs.description: This is a colorized map of the original north polar surface slope of the Moon at a resolution of 16 m/pix by 16 m/pix, based on altimetry data acquired by the LOLA instrument. The LOLA Laser 1 and 2 data through mission phase LRO_SM_17 are the source for this data set.  The bi-directional slope was calculated from a plane fit to three successive laser shots requiring n=5 to 15 profile returns. Depending on orbital velocity, probability of detection, and spacecraft altitude, the slope baseline may vary from 30 to 120 meters.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Average Earth Visibility, 120 mpp, N Pole
docs.description: This data represents the Earth visibility, averaged over hourly timesteps spanning 18.6 years, for the North Polar region of the Moon. Since our light source is not a point but rather a finite disc, its position and size can be changed to study the visibility of the Earth from the lunar poles rather than the solar input. The extent of this data is 75N-90N and has a resolution of 120 m/px. Pixel values represent the percentage of Earth visibility and the legend coveys the mapping colors to values. When using this data please cite: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography, Icarus, Vol. 211, pp. 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030.

docs.title: LRO DLRE Surface Temp Avg N Pole, Color
docs.description: Diviner will characterize temperature variations as a function of latitude, longitude, time of day and season. Diviner will have the capability to make accurate radiometric measurements for the warmest and coldest surfaces on the planet, as well as simultaneous measurements of broadband solar reflectance. The Diviner dataset should be sufficiently complete to allow confident prediction of lunar surface temperatures in daytime, nighttime and polar thermal environments.

docs.title: LRO DLRE, Rock Abundance North Polar
docs.projection:
PROJCS["PolarStereographic Moon", 
	GEOGCS["GCS_Moon", 
		DATUM["D_Moon", 
			SPHEROID["Moon",1737400,0]
		], 
		PRIMEM["Reference_Meridian",0], 
		UNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]
	], 
	PROJECTION["Polar_Stereographic"], 
	PARAMETER["latitude_of_origin",90], 
	PARAMETER["central_meridian",0], 
	PARAMETER["scale_factor",1], 
	PARAMETER["false_easting",0], 
	PARAMETER["false_northing",0], 
	UNIT["metre",1, 
		AUTHORITY["EPSG","9001"]
	]
]
docs.description: This is a colorized global rock abundance map of the north pole region of the lunar surface at 128 pixels per degree. This data is a Level 3 derived Gridded Data Record (GDR) and only contains data collected from October 3, 2009 through October 7, 2011, which corresponds to the mapping orbit phase of the LRO mission.  These data were acquired during near-circular orbits at ˜50 km altitude, which are generally lower altitudes than (typical) elliptical orbits. All GDRs: Each sample represents the areal fraction of the surface covered by rock fragments as estimated using the original algorithm described in Bandfield et al. (2011) with improvements to the algorith accounting for local slopes described in Bandfield et al. (2016). Values are scaled by the value of SCALING_FACTOR. Conversion from Digital Number (DN) to average is given by the equation: RA = (DN * SCALING_FACTOR) + OFFSET Data were restricted to local times or 1930 to 0530 with the solar incidence angles greater than 90 degrees, latitudes between 80N and 80S, emission angles less than 15 degrees, brightness temperatures less than 200K. Local slopes are taken into account using the LROC 128ppd DEM to adjust nighttime rock temperatures used in the model. Several data quality constraints were used as well (quality flag for calibration, 0; quality flag for miscellaneous, 0; noise quality flag, 0 to 1). Gridded level 2 data from diviner spectral channels 6, 7, and 8 binned at 128 pixels per degree. Because of the groundtrack walk and local time drift of Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter observations, most surfaces are covered by only a single observation.  In some cases, surfaces are covered by multiple observations acquired ˜6 or 12 months apart.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Color Hillshade 128ppd, Endurance-A Concept Site P
docs.description: This is a colorized shaded-relief of the original LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM) version 4 cropped to a 50x50 km region for the Endurance-A Site P. The DEM is a shape map (radius) of the Moon at a resolution of 128 pixels per degree, based on altimetry data acquired through September 2011 by the LOLA instrument. The ground tracks were interpolated using the Generic Mapping Tools programs surface and grdblend. The map is in the form of a binary table with one row for each 0.007813 degree of latitude, pixel registered. Map values are referred to a radius of 1737400 m.

docs.title: LRO Mini-RF CPR, S Pole v2
docs.description: This dataset is the Mini-RF Circular Polarization Ratio (CPR) data product. CPR is defined as the ratio of the same sense circular polarization to the opposite sense circular polarization (CPR = SC / OS). The Level 3 products are Derived Data Records (DDRs) generated from multiple Level 2 CDRs.  They are mosaics that are produced by ingesting the Level 2 Stokes 1 parameter and circular polarization files into the ISIS software.  The mosaics are produced for entire lunar globe (i.e., regions between -180 and 180 longitude and -90 to 90 latitude). Unlike the lower-level products, these are composed of data sets collected during multiple acquisitions and are produced manually using the ISIS software provided by the Astrogeology branch of the USGS. The original global dataset was obtained from the Planetary Data System (PDS) at a resolution of 128ppd. docs.title: LRO Mini-RF CPR, S Pole, Colorized v2

docs.title: Ice Stability at Depth Paleo NP
docs.description: The Diviner imaging radiometer experiment aboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed that surface temperatures in parts of the lunar polar regions are among the lowest in the solar system. Moreover, modeling of these Diviner data using realistic thermal conductivity profiles for lunar regolith and topography-based illumination reveals that large expanses of circumpolar terrain could have near-subsurface temperatures well below 110K, despite receiving episodic low-angle solar illumination. These subsurface cold traps could provide areally extensive reservoirs of volatiles. Thermal model results can be used to estimate the stability of water ice deposits to loss by sublimation and diffusive migration through the lunar regolith and map of the depths at which water ice would be lost at a rate of less than 1 kg m-2 per billion years, which corresponds to a loss rate of 1 mm per billion years for a pure ice deposit. The results show that surface cold traps for water ice are surrounded by much more extensive “lunar permafrost” regions where water ice is stable in close proximity to the surface. However, the polar hydrogen deposits mapped by orbiting neutron spectrometers and their observed spatial distribution does not match the expected distribution of water ice inferred from present-day lunar temperatures. This distribution of polar hydrogen preserves evidence that the spin axis of the Moon has shifted, in what is termed true polar wander. This map shows Matt Siegler's calculation of the ice stability depth when the ancient pole was offset toward Cabeus, before true polar wander took place. [Paige, D. A., et al. (2010), Diviner observations of cold traps in the lunar south polar region: Spatial distribution and temperature, Science,330,479–482; Elphic, R, et al. (2011). Limits on the Abundance and Burial Depth of Lunar Polar Ice. AGU Fall Meeting Abstracts; Siegler, M.A, et al. (2016), Lunar true polar wander inferred from polar hydrogen, Nature 531, 480–484]

docs.title: LOLA Permanently Shadowed Regions Northpole 240m
docs.description: This data product is a map of the permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) in the lunar North Pole. The map resolution is 240m/pix by 240m/pix, true at the pole in polar stereographic (spherical) projection. The calculations are based on the LOLA elevation map LDEM_75N_240M and are described in. The values are binary, indicating whether a pixel is in permanent shadow (1) or not (0, NoDATA).

docs.title: LOLA Roughness Northpole 240m, Colorized
docs.description: This is a colorized version of the original north polar surface roughness map for the Moon at a resolution of 240m/pixel, based on altimetry data acquired by the LOLA instrument. The LOLA Laser 1 and 2 data through mission phase LRO_SM_17 are the source for this data set. The residual standard deviation of altitudes from three successive laser shots with n-3 degrees of freedom after fitting a plane to n=5 to 15 profile returns, is averaged in each pixel. Depending on orbital velocity, probability of detection, and spacecraft altitude, the slope baseline may vary from 30 to 120 meters.

docs.title: LRO DLRE Seasonal Difference Max Temp, S Pole
docs.description:
This is the seasonal difference in maximum temperature on the south pole of the Moon. This data was created by subtracting the maximum winter temperature data from the maximum summer temperature data. This data has been obtained from the Diviner instrument onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Obiter (LRO) and is sampled at 240 m/px. The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment is a nine-channel infrared radiometer employing filter radiometry. These channels are distributed between two identical, boresighted telescopes, and an articulated elevation/azimuth mount allows the telescopes to view the lunar surface, space, and calibration targets. The instantaneous field-of-view (FOV) response of each channel is defined by a linear, 21-element, thermopile detector array at the telescope focal plane, and its spectral response is defined by a focal plane bandpass filter. Diviner nadir-pointing RDR data from July, 5, 2009 to Feb 17, 2019 has been compiled into polar stereographic maps of temperatures poleward of 80 degrees latitude at fixed local times and fixed subsolar longitudes to provide an overview of diurnal temperatures of the polar regions. The data has been divided into winter and summer seasons, defined by the times of year when the subsolar latitude is above or below the equator, to characterize the variations in seasonal temperatures that result from the 1.54 degree angle between the Moon's spin pole and the ecliptic plane.

Reference:  Williams, J.-P., B. T. Greenhagen, D. A. Paige, N. Schorghofer, E. Sefton-Nash, P. O. Hayne, P. G. Lucey, M. A. Siegler, and K.-Michael Aye (2019) Seasonal polar temperatures on the Moon, Journal of Geophysical Research, 124, 2505-2521, https://doi.org/10.1029/2019JE006028.

docs.title: LRO DLRE, Anisothermality NP
docs.description: This product depicts the difference between two night time Diviner brightness temperature estimates, one from Channel 7 (25 - 50 micrometer), another from Channel 8 (50 - 100 micrometer). The difference is pronounced after sunset and presumably all through the nightside due to anisothermality in the scene. That is, the pixels are actually viewing a mixture of surface temperatures, and each channel integrates across a different part of the summed black body spectra. Differences, Tb7 – Tb8, reveal the presence of high-thermal-inertia features, i.e., rocks. The units are Kelvins. Only values where Tb7 and Tb8 are greater than 50K and less than 150K are considered valid. Missing or otherwise invalid values are –999. The data are from 2000 LT, two hours LT after sunset. This represents early evening local LT, when rockier areas are warmest during their diurnal cool-down, and rocks will be noticeably warmer than fine regolith.

docs.title: LRO LAMP Albedo N Pole, Color
docs.description: The Lyman Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) is a far-ultraviolet (FUV) imaging spectrograph on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) mission. Its main objectives are to (i) identify and localize exposed water frost in permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), (ii) characterize landforms and albedos in PSRs, (iii) demonstrate the feasibility of using natural starlight and sky-glow illumination for future lunar surface mission applications, and (iv) characterize the lunar atmosphere and its variability. As a byproduct, LAMP will map a large fraction of the Moon at FUV wavelengths, allowing new studies of the microphysical and reflectance properties of the regolith. The LAMP FUV spectrograph will accomplish these objectives by measuring the signal reflected from the night-side lunar surface and in PSRs using both the interplanetary HI Lyman-alpha sky-glow and FUV starlight as light sources. Both these light sources provide fairly uniform, but faint, illumination. With the expected LAMP sensitivity, by the end of the primary 1-year LRO mission, the SNR for a Lyman-alpha albedo map should be greater than 100 in polar regions greater than 1 km2, providing useful FUV constraints to help characterize subtle compositional and structural features.

docs.title: LRO LOLA Average Earth Visibility, 240 mpp, N Pole
docs.description: This data represents the Earth visibility, averaged over hourly timesteps spanning 18.6 years, for the North Polar region of the Moon. Since our light source is not a point but rather a finite disc, its position and size can be changed to study the visibility of the Earth from the lunar poles rather than the solar input. The extent of this data has been clipped to 60N-90N and has a resolution of 240 m/px. Pixel values represent the percentage of Earth visibility and the legend coveys the mapping colors to values. When using this data please cite: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography, Icarus, Vol. 211, pp. 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030.

docs.description: This is a colorized representation of the sky visibility (solid angle not obscured by topography as seen from the surface), for the North Polar region of the moon. docs.title: LRO LOLA Color Sky Visibility, 240 mpp, S Pole
docs.description: This is a colorized representation of the sky visibility (solid angle not obscured by topography as seen from the surface), for the South Polar region of the moon. Since our light source is not a point but rather a finite disc, its position and size can be changed to study the visibility of the sky from the lunar poles rather than the solar input. The extent of this data has been clipped to 60S-90S and has a resolution of 240 m/px. Pixel values represent the sky visibility measured by the steradian (sr); the Standard International (SI) unit of solid angular measure. There are 4 pi, or approximately 12.5664, steradians in a complete sphere. The legend coveys the mapping colors to values. When using this data please cite: Mazarico, E., et al. (2011), Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography, Icarus, Vol. 211, pp. 1066-1081, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.10.030.

docs.title: LP NS Colorized Water Equivalent Hydrogen NP
docs.description: This colorized map of Water Equivalent Hydrogen is based on an updated analysis of Lunar Prospector epithermal neutron data. An improved map of the distribution of hydrogen near to the lunar poles was achieved using a specially developed pixon image reconstruction algorithm to deconvolve the instrumental response of the Lunar Prospector's neutron spectrometer from the observed data, while simultaneously suppressing the statistical noise.

docs.title: Kaguya SP Clinopyroxene Abundance NP
docs.description:
This is a map of polar Clinopyroxene abundance. Quantitative lunar polar mineral abundance maps were derived by comparing continuum-removed Kaguya Spectral Profiler (SP) reflectance spectra between 742.8 and 1555.5 nm, to continuum-removed spectra modeled using radiative transfer equations (which describe the scattering of light interacting with intimately mixed particles larger than the wavelength). A composition was then assigned to each SP point by searching for the best spectral match, ensuring that the best spectral fit contains within +/-5 wt.% FeO of the given SP point. FeO abundances were determined using SP and LOLA data as described for the Polar FeO Abundance Maps by Lemelin, et al. (MINERALOGY AND IRON CONTENT OF THE LUNAR POLAR REGIONS USING THE KAGUYA SPECTRAL PROFILER AND THE LUNAR ORBITER LASER ALTIMETER. M. Lemelin, P. G. Lucey, K. Jha, and D. Trang, Lunar and Planetary Science XLVIII, 2017)

The Kaguya Spectral Profiler was a nadir looking visible - near infrared spectrometer onboard the Japanese SELENE (Kaguya) lunar explorer launched in September 2007. SP consisted of one reflective telescope, two plane gratings, three linear detectors, one three-stage peltier cooler, and two halogen lamps with a filter for radiometric and spectral calibration. Its spectral coverage and sampling interval, 0.5 - 2.6 !m and 6 - 8 nm, were optimized for the detection of spectral absorption features of lunar surface minerals. The along-track sampling interval was 500 m. The total number of SP's spectral channels was 296 including several overlapping channels around 1 micrometer.

docs.title: LRO LOLA and Kaguya SP FeO Abundance NP
docs.description:
This is a map of polar iron oxide (FeO) abundance. FeO maps of the polar regions (50-90 degree in latitude) at 1 km per pixel were derived by taking advantage of calibrated reflectance data at 1064 nm from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) and using it along with the 955.5/752.8 nm reflectance ratio from the Kaguya Spectral Profiler (SP). (MINERALOGY AND IRON CONTENT OF THE LUNAR POLAR REGIONS USING THE KAGUYA SPECTRAL PROFILER AND THE LUNAR ORBITER LASER ALTIMETER. M. Lemelin, P. G. Lucey, K. Jha3, and D. Trang, Lunar and Planetary Science XLVIII, 2017)

The Kaguya Spectral Profiler was a nadir looking visible - near infrared spectrometer onboard the Japanese SELENE (Kaguya) lunar explorer launched in September 2007. SP consisted of one reflective telescope, two plane gratings, three linear detectors, one three-stage peltier cooler, and two halogen lamps with a filter for radiometric and spectral calibration. Its spectral coverage and sampling interval, 0.5 - 2.6 !m and 6 - 8 nm, were optimized for the detection of spectral absorption features of lunar surface minerals. The along-track sampling interval was 500 m. The total number of SP's spectral channels was 296 including several overlapping channels around 1 micrometer.

The Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboart the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has been actively acquiring reflectance data of the Moon since 2009; it sends a laser pulse towards the Moon at 1064 nm and measures the energy returned from the surface at 0 degree phase angle, regardless of the Sun’s illumination conditions. It provides high signal to noise ratio for the entire lunar surface, regardless of topography, and has been thoroughly calibrated and gridded into polar maps of 1 km per pixel.
docs.instrument: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter and Spectral Profiler

docs.title: GRAIL LGRS, Bouguer Disturbances L1200
docs.description: This data product is a map of the   Bouguer disturbances (in mGal) of the lunar gravity field at a resolution  of 16 pix/deg by 16 pix/deg. It is based on a GRAIL gravity field of the Moon  produced by NASA GSFC called GRGM1200A. GRGM1200A is a degree and order 1200  spherical harmonic model, which includes the entire mission of GRAIL tracking  data. The LOLA topography, expressed in the Principal Axes frame, was used to  remove the contribution of the lunar relief (assuming a constant density of  2500 kg/m3). The Bouguer disturbances are expanded in the spatial domain up   to degree and order 1200.   Some details describing this model are:    The spherical harmonic coefficients are fully normalized (geodesy 4pi    normalized).    The uncertainties are calibrated (the formal uncertainties multiplied by    a factor of 1.635).    The reference radius = 1738.0 km    The gravitational parameter is GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2    The planetary ephemeris used is de430 and defines the lunar body-fixed        coordinate system.    A Kaula type power law constraint is applied to the spherical harmonics        coefficients for degrees >600 (3.6e-4/n^2).    The weighting of the KBRR data is:        0.03 microns/sec in the primary mission        0.05 microns/sec in the extended mission    The weighting of the DSN data is:        0.12mm/s in both the primary and extended mission   The nominal tidal Love number is k2 = 0.024133 +/- 0.000016   The current best reference for the GRGM1200A gravity field is  LEMOINEETAL2014, published in the Geophysical Research Letters with the  DOI number 10.1002/2014GL060027 . For additional details on the GRAIL  mission, data and methods, see LEMOINEETAL2013.     Each point gives the Lunar Bouguer gravity disturbance in milligals,    on a reference sphere with semi-major-axis = 1738.0 km,    GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2, and zero rotation rate.   As with other lunar gravity fields, the map is expressed in the Moon  Principal Axes frame, which slightly differs from the Moon Mean Earth frame.  For comparison with lunar topography, users are advised to make use of   the LOLA PDS products also archived in the Moon Principal Axes frame, such  as the LDEM_64_PA product in the LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0 dataset, which   can be accessed at the PDS Geosciences Node or at the LOLA PDS Data node.  Note also that the reference radius for gravity (1738 km) and topography  (1737.4 km) are different."

For additional details on the GRAIL  mission, data and methods, see LEMOINEETAL2013.     Each point gives the Lunar gravity disturbance in milligals,    on a reference sphere with semi-major-axis = 1738.0 km,    GM = 4902.80011526323 km**3/s**2, and zero rotation rate.   As other lunar gravity fields, the map is expressed in the Moon Principal  Axes frame, which slightly differs from the Moon Mean Earth frame. docs.title: LRO DLRE Bolometric Brightness Max Temperature Anomalies, 0.5 ppd, N Pole
docs.description:
The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has been acquiring solar reflectance and mid-infrared radiance measurements nearly continuously since July of 2009. Approximately a quarter trillion calibrated radiance measurements of the Moon, acquired over the first 5.5 years of the mission, have been compiled into our Level 4 - Global Cumulative Products (GCP). This data represents a compilation of all Diviner nadir observations from 5-July-2009 to 1-April-2015. They are produced by binning Diviner RDR (Level 1b) radiance measurements for each IR channel (channels 3-9) in 0.5 degree bins in longitude and latitude, and 0.25 hours of local time to determine the average brightness temperatures on a global cylindrical grid. Additionally, the average radiance values for all the channels were used to determine the bolometric brightness temperatures for each bin.

This map represents the maximum temperatures anomalies with zonal mean subtracted at 0.5 ppd. Maximum temperature variations are related to albedo. The average temperatures for given latitude subtracted out (zonal average removed) highlight anomalous temperatures due to variations in the regolith properties as well as the ratios and the difference between the minimum and maximum temperatures which highlight the relative differences between the two temperature extremes and the amplitude of the extremes in temperature. For more information, please refer to: Williams, J. P., Paige, D. A., Greenhagen, B. T., & Sefton-Nash, E. (2017). The global surface temperatures of the moon as measured by the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment. Icarus, 283, 300-325.

docs.title: LRO DLRE Bolometric Brightness Temperature RGB Composite, 0.5 ppd, N Pole
docs.description:
The Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment onboard the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has been acquiring solar reflectance and mid-infrared radiance measurements nearly continuously since July of 2009. Approximately a quarter trillion calibrated radiance measurements of the Moon, acquired over the first 5.5 years of the mission, have been compiled into our Level 4 - Global Cumulative Products (GCP). This data represents a compilation of all Diviner nadir observations from 5-July-2009 to 1-April-2015. They are produced by binning Diviner RDR (Level 1b) radiance measurements for each IR channel (channels 3-9) in 0.5 degree bins in longitude and latitude, and 0.25 hours of local time to determine the average brightness temperatures on a global cylindrical grid. Additionally, the average radiance values for all the channels were used to determine the bolometric brightness temperatures for each bin.

This RGB composite map allows for broad characterization of terrains based on minimum and maximum temperatures (normalized by zonal mean temperatures). Maximum temperatures are sensitive to the radiative properties of the surface and minimum temperatures are sensitive to the thermophysical properties of the regolith. This characterization is highlighted in an RGB composite map (±70° latitude) where the red channel is visual brightness derived from Diviner’s visible channel (channel 1), the green channel is the minimum temperaures, and the blue channel is the maximum temperatures. Terrains can be characterized as low/high reflectance and low/high thermal inertia (TI). Young craters and rays (yellow/orange) are bright and high TI. Cold spots and radar dark halos (magenta) are bright and low TI, mare (cyan/blue) are dark and high TI, pyroclastic deposits (blue) are dark and low TI. For more information, please refer to: Williams, J. P., Paige, D. A., Greenhagen, B. T., & Sefton-Nash, E. (2017). The global surface temperatures of the moon as measured by the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment. Icarus, 283, 300-325.

docs.title: GRAIL LGRS, Crust-mantle Interface Depth Model 1
docs.description: High-resolution gravity data obtained from the dual Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) spacecraft show that the bulk density of the Moon’s highlands crust is 2550 kilograms per cubic meter, substantially lower than generally assumed. When combined with remote sensing and sample data, this density implies an average crustal porosity of 12% to depths of at least a few kilometers. Lateral variations in crustal porosity correlate with the largest impact basins, whereas lateral variations in crustal density correlate with crustal composition. The low-bulk crustal density allows construction of a global crustal thickness model that satisfies the Apollo seismic constraints, and with an average crustal thickness between 34 and 43 kilometers, the bulk refractory element composition of the Moon is not required to be enriched with respect to that of Earth.

docs.title: LP NS Water Equivalent Hydrogen NP
docs.description: This map of Water Equivalent Hydrogen is based on an updated analysis of Lunar Prospector epithermal neutron data. An improved map of the distribution of hydrogen near to the lunar poles was achieved using a specially developed pixon image reconstruction algorithm to deconvolve the instrumental response of the Lunar Prospector's neutron spectrometer from the observed data, while simultaneously suppressing the statistical noise.

docs.title: LP MAG ER Bphi Component Magnetic Field 2ppd
docs.description: This dataset is a global model of the lunar crustal Bphi component magnetic field, evaluated at the surface of the Moon, from Ravat et al. (2020, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets). It was derived from Lunar Prospector (LP) Magnetometer/Electron Reflectometer (MAG/ER) magnetometer data using along-track vector field differences. The field is represented with magnetic monopole bases and constrained by L1-norm regularization of the radial component (Br) at the surface. Monopoles remain stable at closer spacing than dipoles, improving spatial resolution, and L1-norm regularization favors sparse models suited to the Moon’s localized anomalies. Values are in nanotesla (nT) with a pixel resolution of 0.5 degree spacing. Longitude has been converted from 0° to 360° to -180° to 180°.

(2020, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets). It was derived from Lunar Prospector (LP) Magnetometer/Electron Reflectometer (MAG/ER) magnetometer data using along-track vector field differences. The field is represented with magnetic monopole bases and constrained by L1-norm regularization of the radial component (Br) at the surface. Monopoles remain stable at closer spacing than dipoles, improving spatial resolution, and L1-norm regularization favors sparse models suited to the Moon’s localized anomalies. Values are in nanotesla (nT) with a pixel resolution of 0.5 degree spacing. Longitude has been converted from 0° to 360° to -180° to 180°.
